title: Broken oaths
hookLine: he reproaches the emperor's officers who swore safe passage and broke it (Zafarnama)

cards: A promise is the cheapest thing in the world to make. It costs a breath. It is also one of the few things that can't be bought back once it's broken.
Tradition tells it like this. Anandpur had been under siege for a long time. Food was gone.

Word came from the emperor's side: leave the fort, and you will have safe passage. Oaths were sworn, tradition says, on what each side held holy. The Guru's household and his Sikhs went out into the night.
And once they were out, the armies fell on them. The praise is finished. In the next stretch of his letter, Guru Gobind Singh turns to the oath.

teach.h: I HAD NO TRUST IN YOUR OATH.
teach.b: The Zafarnama is written in Persian verse, and this part of it is plain speaking. Paraphrased, the Guru says: I had no trust in your oath. Your officers swore in God's name, and their words were false.
A man who breaks his oath, he writes, cannot be trusted with anything. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't curse the emperor's faith.

teach.h: HE HOLDS THE EMPEROR TO HIS OWN FAITH.
teach.b: He holds the emperor to it. You call on God, he says, in effect; then keep the promises you make in God's name. The standard he reaches for is one the emperor already claims.
That makes the letter harder to wave away, because it isn't an outsider's insult. It's a mirror. Some readers notice that the letter is written after terrible loss, and yet the charge is precise.
Not you are evil, but you gave your word and broke it.
A grievance that names one clear wrong can be answered. A grievance that names everything usually can't. And for Sikhs the oath runs the other way too.
In the Gurus' teaching, truthful living stands above clever speech, and the Khalsa is asked to be someone whose word holds.
The Zafarnama's anger at broken oaths is also a picture of the opposite: a person, or a people, who keep theirs. Look back over the week. Sparks from one fire.
The wondrous drama. Only the servant. Through the battle at Bhangani.
Head, not faith. Begin with praise. Read together, they sketch one person: a servant who praises first, names the cost, and stands behind his words.

how: Sikhs read and recite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, and its lines on broken oaths are often recalled in katha and in teaching about truthful living and keeping one's word.

o: vows a soldier takes when joining an army
promises sworn in God's name, then betrayed
curses spoken against an enemy in battle

games.q: the letter and the oath: tap the pairs.
p: safe passage if they left the fort
I had no trust in your oath

s: in the Zafarnama, the Guru attacks the emperor's religion
he holds the emperor to it: one who calls on God should keep promises made in God's name.
the letter names one clear wrong: an oath sworn and broken
the charge is precise, not a list of insults.
the Zafarnama is written in Punjabi prose
it is written in Persian verse.

games.q: you've been betrayed by people who swore an oath in God's name. you're writing to the man in charge of them. how do you make the charge?
o: hold them to the faith they already claim.
games.why: Guru Gobind Singh holds the emperor to his own standard: a promise made in God's name should be kept. that makes it a mirror, not an insult.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open, a call you said you'd return, something you told a child, and hold it without scolding yourself, like a ticket you haven't used yet.
If you pray, hold that promise before Waheguru as you breathe out.

wordCard.voice: Broken oaths. In the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh tells the emperor he had no trust in an oath sworn in God's name and then broken. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, the Zafarnama's language: an oath. the Guru writes that he had no trust in their oath.

carryVoice: Your line: keep your oath. A promise costs a breath to make. That's the week.

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), the verses on the oath and its breaking
